summary: Describes how to send Hebrew in electronic mail, using MIME and the ISO-8859-8 character set.

eli5.summary: Hebrew is written right to left with its own letters. This memo says which letter code to use so email shows it properly.

questions: how to send hebrew text in email
subtitle: Encoding and sending Hebrew text in electronic mail.

tldr.problem: Email systems needed a standard way to represent Hebrew characters, which use the right-to-left writing direction and require more than ASCII can express.
tldr.mechanism: Hebrew text is translated to ISO-8859-8 (the Latin/Hebrew alphabet standard) and then encoded using either Quoted-Printable or Base64 encoding with MIME headers specifying the character set.
tldr.outcome: Users in Israel and elsewhere can now send Hebrew email reliably, with MIME headers telling mail clients how to decode and display the text correctly.

today: RFC 1555 established the standard for Hebrew in email, which remains in use. The visual directionality model and the use of ISO-8859-8 have seen adoption in Israeli and international Hebrew mail, though modern systems often use UTF-8 instead. RFC 1556 (Handling of Bi-directional Texts) is the companion specification for more complex text direction scenarios.

sections.title: Hebrew and Email
sections.content: Electronic mail using RFC 822 format did not inherently support Hebrew, which has its own alphabet and runs from right to left (opposite to English). The RFC describes the standard method for sending Hebrew in email by using MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) and the ISO-8859-8 character set. The document includes a detailed conversion table showing how the four most common Hebrew encodings (PC 8-bit ASCII, IBM EBCDIC, PC 7-bit ASCII, and ISO-8859-8) map to the same Hebrew letters.
sections.eli5: Email was designed for English, which uses only simple letters. Hebrew needs its own number codes.

sections.title: The ISO-8859-8 Encoding
sections.content: Hebrew text must first be translated to ISO-8859-8, an 8-bit character set. Hebrew letters like alef, bet, and gimel map to byte values 224 through 250. The standard notes that ISO-8859-8 is also known as IBM Codepage 862. Hebrew text is then encoded using either Quoted-Printable (preferred for readability) or Base64 encoding, as defined by MIME, before being transmitted.
sections.eli5: Hebrew letters get converted to numbers, then those numbers get encoded in a way email can carry.

sections.title: MIME Headers and Directionality
sections.content: Mail containing Hebrew must include MIME headers specifying the character set and transfer encoding: MIME-Version: 1.0, Content-type: text/plain; charset=ISO-8859-8, and Content-transfer-encoding: BASE64 or Quoted-Printable. By default, the text direction is visual: Hebrew text is encoded left-to-right (even though Hebrew is read right-to-left) and transmitted left-to-right via MIME. The complementary RFC 1556 covers explicit and implicit directionality modes for bidirectional text and mixed scripts like Hebrew and English on the same line.
sections.eli5: The email headers say 'this is Hebrew' and how to decode it. The text itself is stored left-to-right for simplicity.
